text: Unbounded parser buffer growth in JsonTokenizer.fillBuf(): a single oversized JSON token drives repeated capacity doubling with no ceiling, giving attacker-controlled memory exhaustion. Attacker input enters at `reader.read(buf, storeEnd, buf.length - storeEnd)` (JsonTokenizer.java:495). readString() accumulates the token body into `buf[storeEnd++]` (lines 152-154) without ever flushing, so the stored-token length grows with the attacker's token. Once `storeLen == buf.length` (line 475), fillBuf() executes `char[] doubleBuf = Arrays.copyOf(buf, 2 * buf.length)` (line 477) -- there is no maximum-capacity check anywhere on this path. A client POSTing one JSON document containing a single huge string value (e.g. {"a":"AAAA..."}) therefore forces the char[] to double repeatedly until OutOfMemoryError. Confirmed there is no bounding config: org.eclipse.parsson.api.JsonConfig declares only MAX_BIGINTEGER_SCALE, MAX_BIGDECIMAL_LEN, MAX_DEPTH and REJECT_DUPLICATE_KEYS -- no string-length, token-length or document-size limit exists to cap this allocation.

The MAX_BIGDECIMAL_LEN mitigation is enforced too late to prevent the memory cost it was added to stop. JsonTokenizer.getBigDecimal() rejects oversized numeric literals at line 521 (`sourceLen > jsonContext.bigDecimalLengthLimit()` -> UnsupportedOperationException, default 1100 chars), but that check runs only at BigDecimal *conversion* time. By then readNumber()/readNumberChar() -> read() -> fillBuf() have already buffered the entire numeric token and grown `buf` by unbounded doubling (line 477). So a JSON document containing one gigantic numeric literal (e.g. a 500MB run of digits) exhausts memory during tokenization and never reaches the length check -- and if the parser is driven with nextToken()/getString() rather than getBigDecimal(), the check is never consulted at all. The limit guards only the `new BigDecimal(buf, storeBegin, sourceLen)` CPU cost, not the buffering allocation.
evidence:
Q1 (the check and its location): MATCH (c:CpgCall {scan_id:$scan_id}) WHERE c.code CONTAINS 'bigDecimalLengthLimit' OR c.code CONTAINS 'depthLimit' RETURN c.name, c.code, c.file_path, c.line, c.reachable_from_entry, c.hop_distance
-> JsonTokenizer.java:521 {name:'<operator>.greaterThan', code:'sourceLen > jsonContext.bigDecimalLengthLimit()', uid:'87e4a3a6170417d6068d14663c71ffb2fa833c70', reach:true, hop:5}; JsonTokenizer.java:522 {code:'new UnsupportedOperationException(String.format("Number of BigDecimal source characters %d exceeded maximal allowed value of %d", sourceLen, jsonContext.bigDecimalLengthLimit()))', reach:true, hop:5}. The only occurrences of bigDecimalLengthLimit in the whole scan are JsonContext.java:78/95/117 (assignment + accessor) and JsonTokenizer.java:521-525 -- it appears nowhere in fillBuf/readNumber.

Q2 (source text of the guarded method): semantic_search 'tokenizer read number BigDecimal length limit exceeded max value' -> JsonTokenizer.java:518-557: 'BigDecimal getBigDecimal() { if (bd == null) { int sourceLen = storeEnd - storeBegin; if (sourceLen > jsonContext.bigDecimalLengthLimit()) { throw new UnsupportedOperationException(...); } bd = new BigDecimal(buf, storeBegin, sourceLen); } return bd; }' -- confirming the check is on the already-buffered storeBegin..storeEnd range, i.e. after buffering.

Q3 (buffering happens first, unbounded): MATCH (c:CpgCall) WHERE c.file_path ENDS WITH 'JsonTokenizer.java' AND c.line >= 465 AND c.line <= 500 -> line 477 {name:'copyOf', code:'copyOf(buf, 2 * buf.length)', reach:true, hop:9} with no limit comparison in that range.

Q4 (chain number-token -> fillBuf): MATCH (m:CpgMethod)-[:CONTAINS_CALL]->(c:CpgCall)-[:RESOLVES_TO]->(t:CpgMethod) WHERE m.file_path ENDS WITH 'JsonTokenizer.java' -> {caller:'nextToken', call:'this.readNumber(ch)', line:389}; {caller:'readNumberChar', call:'this.read()', line:219}; {caller:'read', call:'this.fillBuf()', line:456}. getBigDecimal is only called from getInt (line 543), getLong (line 558), isIntegral (line 577) -- all optional, so the limit can be skipped entirely.

text: An attacker-inflated tokenizer buffer is retained indefinitely in a shared, uncapped buffer pool, turning a transient spike into persistent memory retention. After fillBuf() has doubled `buf` to an attacker-chosen size, JsonTokenizer.close() hands that oversized array to the shared pool via `jsonContext.bufferPool().recycle(buf)` (JsonTokenizer.java:583). BufferPoolImpl.recycle() is simply `getQueue().offer(t)` -- it performs no size cap on the queue and no check that the returned array is the standard 4096-char size it hands out in take(). Because the default pool is shared across parsers/requests, multi-megabyte buffers from hostile documents accumulate in the ConcurrentLinkedQueue and are only reclaimable when the WeakReference wrapping the whole queue is cleared, so memory is not released after the offending request completes. fillBuf() at line 478 likewise recycles the pre-doubling buffer on every growth step, offering progressively larger arrays into the same unbounded queue.

Attacker-controlled JSON request bodies are written unsanitized to the process log in the JAX-RS demo handlers, allowing log forging/injection. ArrayResource.doPost (an :EntryPoint, exposure='reachable') receives a parsed JsonStructure from the HTTP request body and passes it straight to System.out.println(structure) at ArrayResource.java:42. The same pattern appears at ObjectResource.java:53 and StructureResource.java:52. Because JsonStructure.toString() reproduces attacker-supplied string contents, an attacker who embeds newline/CR characters in JSON string values can inject forged log records. Note this is reached via the structure's toString(), not via JsonGeneratorImpl's escaping path, so the generator's control-character escaping does not apply. These are demo modules rather than the shipped impl/ library, which caps real-world impact.

JsonTokenizer has NO maximum token/string length control: fillBuf() doubles the internal char[] without any upper bound (`char[] doubleBuf = Arrays.copyOf(buf, 2 * buf.length)`), so a single oversized JSON string token drives unbounded heap allocation. The only length control in the library, bigDecimalLengthLimit, is applied in getBigDecimal() at line 521 — i.e. AFTER the buffer has already been grown to hold the whole token — and it covers numbers only, never strings. JsonContext exposes no max-string-length / max-token-length property at all (its entire control surface is depthLimit, bigIntegerScaleLimit, bigDecimalLengthLimit, prettyPrinting, rejectDuplicateKeys, bufferPool). Aggravating factor: the grown buffer is handed back to the shared pool via `jsonContext.bufferPool().recycle(buf)` at line 583, so one oversized document permanently inflates the process-wide BufferPool. This sits on the core untrusted-input path (JsonReaderImpl/JsonParserImpl -> JsonTokenizer), including the JAX-RS JsonValueBodyReader.
evidence: Query: MATCH (c:CpgCall {scan_id:$scan_id}) WHERE c.file_path CONTAINS 'JsonTokenizer' AND (c.code CONTAINS 'Arrays.copyOf' OR c.code CONTAINS 'buf.length' OR c.code CONTAINS 'bufferPool') RETURN c.line, c.name, c.code -> line 125 `this.buf = jsonContext.bufferPool().take()`; line 475 `storeLen == buf.length`; line 477 `char[] doubleBuf = Arrays.copyOf(buf, 2 * buf.length)` with NO comparison against any limit; line 478 `this.jsonContext.bufferPool().recycle(buf)`; line 583 `this.jsonContext.bufferPool().recycle(buf)`. semantic_search('JsonTokenizer resize buffer doubling array copyOf') returned fillBuf() source: `if (storeLen == buf.length) { // buffer is full, double the capacity  char[] doubleBuf = Arrays.copyOf(buf, 2 * buf.length); ... }` — no max-size guard. Contrast query over the same file lines 500-600 shows the ONLY length check is for numbers: line 521 `sourceLen > jsonContext.bigDecimalLengthLimit()` inside getBigDecimal(), reached only after the token is fully buffered. semantic_search('JsonConfig configuration property names MAX_DEPTH REJECT_DUPLICATE_KEYS maximum limits') returned the complete JsonContext accessor set (bigIntegerScaleLimit, bigDecimalLengthLimit, depthLimit, prettyPrinting, rejectDuplicateKeys, bufferPool) — no string/token length limit exists.

text: JsonPatchImpl.DiffGenerator.diffArray() allocates a quadratic LCS matrix `int[][] c = new int[m+1][n+1]` where m and n are the sizes of the two attacker-supplied JSON arrays, with NO size cap or product check anywhere. There is no configurable limit for this in JsonConfig/JsonContext at all (unlike depth and number length), so Json.createDiff(source, target) on two moderately large arrays allocates m*n ints: two 50,000-element arrays request ~2.5e9 ints (~10 GB) and OOM the JVM from a request body of only a few hundred KB — a very high amplification factor.
evidence: Query: MATCH (c:CpgCall {scan_id:$scan_id}) WHERE c.file_path CONTAINS 'JsonPatchImpl' AND (c.code CONTAINS 'new int' OR c.code CONTAINS 'size()' OR c.name IN ['diff','diffObject','diffArray']) RETURN c.line, c.name, c.code -> line 270 `int m = source.size()`, line 271 `int n = target.size()`, line 272 `int[][] c = new int[m + 1][n + 1]` with no bounds check between the size() reads and the allocation. semantic_search('JsonPatchImpl diff emit recursive LCS array compare path') returned diffArray() source confirming `int m = source.size(); int n = target.size(); int [][] c = new int[m+1][n+1];` immediately followed by the nested fill loops, no guard. Exhaustive control query MATCH (c:CpgCall {scan_id:$scan_id}) WHERE c.name IN ['bigIntegerScaleLimit','bigDecimalLengthLimit','depthLimit','rejectDuplicateKeys'] returned 40 rows, NONE in JsonPatchImpl.java — no limit of any kind is consulted in this file.

text: JsonStructureParser maintains its scope stack as a plain unbounded `new ArrayDeque<>()` and pushes onto it with no depth check, whereas its sibling JsonParserImpl constructs a depth-limited `new Stack(jsonContext.depthLimit())` in all three of its constructors. The MAX_DEPTH control is therefore simply absent from the in-memory parser returned by Json.createParserFactory(config).createParser(JsonStructure) — the configured org.eclipse.parsson.maxDepth property is silently ignored on this path, so walking a deeply nested JsonStructure is unbounded.

Contrast query on JsonParserImpl lines 58-92 -> line 66 `this.stack = new Stack(jsonContext.depthLimit())`, line 72 same, line 79 same. Exhaustive query MATCH (c:CpgCall {scan_id:$scan_id}) WHERE toLower(c.code) CONTAINS 'depth' RETURN c.file_path, c.line, c.code confirms the ONLY depthLimit() consultations in the entire scan are JsonParserImpl lines 66, 72, 79; the `int depth` locals at JsonStructureParser 159/165/168/179/182 are skipObject/skipArray balance counters (`depth++`/`depth--`, compared to `depth > 0`), never compared against any maximum.

text: JsonGeneratorImpl enforces no depth limit on output: its context stack is a plain unbounded `Deque stack = new ArrayDeque<>()` (line 86) pushed by writeStartObject/writeStartArray with no limit check, and write(JsonValue) is directly self-recursive over nested children (line 240 -> 249 `write(child)`; line 312 -> 331 `write(member.getKey(), member.getValue())`) with no depth parameter or counter. jsonContext.depthLimit() is never consulted in this file, so serializing a deeply nested JsonStructure recurses until StackOverflowError. This is reachable from the public writer API: JsonWriterImpl line 67 calls `this.generator.write(value)` in a loop over the structure.

text: JsonMergePatchImpl.mergePatch() recurses once per nesting level of the attacker-supplied patch document (line 78 `mergePatch(targetJsonObject.get(key), value)` and line 80 `mergePatch(JsonValue.EMPTY_JSON_OBJECT, value)`) with no depth counter, depth parameter, or depthLimit() consultation — the MAX_DEPTH control is absent from this file entirely. The same gap exists in the static diff() helper (line 106 `diff(value, t.get(key), jsonContext)`) and in JsonPatchImpl's mutually recursive diff/diffObject (line 236 -> 247 -> back to diff, and line 319). Both JSON Merge Patch (RFC 7386) and JSON Patch diff are applied to two untrusted documents, so a deeply nested patch body recurses to StackOverflowError; note MAX_DEPTH is operator-configurable upward and structures built via JsonObjectBuilder have no depth cap at all, so the recursion bound is not reliably 1000.

JsonPatchImpl query -> line 236 `diffObject(path, (JsonObject) source, (JsonObject) target)`, line 247 `diff(path + '/' + Json.encodePointer(key), value, target.get(key))`, line 319 `diff(path + '/' + (i - 1), source.get(i - 1), target.get(j - 1))`. Exhaustive query MATCH (c:CpgCall {scan_id:$scan_id}) WHERE toLower(c.code) CONTAINS 'depth' returns NO rows for JsonMergePatchImpl.java or JsonPatchImpl.java; the control-consultation query for depthLimit returns only JsonParserImpl 66/72/79.

text: The JAX-RS entity provider JsonValueBodyReader builds its reader factory as `Json.createReaderFactory(null)` — a null config map, meaning no hardening properties (org.eclipse.parsson.maxDepth, maxBigDecimalLength, maxBigIntegerScale, rejectDuplicateKeys) are set for a component whose entire job is deserializing untrusted HTTP request bodies. Parsing therefore relies solely on library defaults (DEFAULT_MAX_DEPTH = 1000), and any limit with no default — notably token/string length, see the JsonTokenizer lead — is unbounded on this attacker-facing path. Reported as the weakest lead because defaults do exist for depth; the missing control is the explicit per-deployment hardening, not depth itself.
evidence: Query: MATCH (c:CpgCall {scan_id:$scan_id}) WHERE c.file_path CONTAINS 'JsonValueBodyReader' OR c.file_path CONTAINS 'JsonValueBodyWriter' RETURN c.file_path, c.line, c.name, c.code -> JsonValueBodyReader line 45 `JsonReaderFactory this.rf = Json.createReaderFactory(null)`, line 69 `this.rf.createReader(inputStream)`, line 70 `readValue()`. Note the sibling writer DOES build a props map (JsonValueBodyWriter line 69 `Map props = new HashMap<>()`, line 71 `put(JsonGenerator.PRETTY_PRINTING, true)`, line 73 `createWriterFactory(props)`), showing config plumbing exists but is passed as null on the read path. Default value grounded by the 'depth' sweep: `int JsonContext.DEFAULT_MAX_DEPTH = 1000` and JsonContext line 79 `this.depthLimit = getIntConfig(JsonConfig.MAX_DEPTH, config, DEFAULT_MAX_DEPTH)`.

text: In demos/twitter/.../TwitterObjectSearch.java, the OAuth 1.0a replay protection is disabled by a hardcoded constant nonce, with a bare `// TODO` comment sitting immediately above it marking the unfinished fix. Inside getSearchStream() (method at line 67), the anonymous TreeMap initializer at line 81 contains: put("oauth_consumer_key", consumerKey); then `// TODO`; then put("oauth_nonce", "4b25256957d75b6370f33a4501dc5e7e");. The nonce is NOT regenerated per request -- it is a fixed 32-hex-char literal. This is not dead code: the same `map` is serialized into paramsString (lines 93-104), folded into the HMAC-SHA1 signature base string (lines 107-113), signed with Mac.getInstance("HmacSHA1") / SecretKeySpec(consumerSecret + "&" + accessTokenSecret) (lines 116-119), the result stored back via map.put("oauth_signature", oauthSig) (line 121), and emitted as the `OAuth ` Authorization header (line 126+). In OAuth 1.0a the nonce+timestamp pair IS the anti-replay control, so every signed request this demo issues reuses the same nonce, making signed requests capture-replayable and defeating the server-side dedup the spec relies on. Classic Shape C: a developer-acknowledged (`// TODO`) protection stubbed to a constant while the surrounding signing path is fully live. Scope caveat for the verifier: this is in the `demos/` tree (a CLI `main` that reads its own config file), so blast radius is limited to the demo/sample code rather than the shipped `impl/` library -- but it is copy-paste reference code in the project's own demos.

Transport protection is applied on two of three outbound-API demo paths and silently omitted on the third, where it also leaks a credential. demos/rest/.../ParserResource.java line 53 builds `new URL("http://api.flickr.com/services/rest/?method=flickr.photos.getRecent&api_key=221160312e1c22ec60ecf336951b0e77&format=json&nojsoncallback=1&per_page=20")` -- plaintext HTTP carrying a hardcoded Flickr api_key in the query string. The sibling demos in the same repo DO use TLS for the identical pattern: TwitterObjectSearch.java:69 `String searchUrl = "https://api.twitter.com/1.1/search/tweets.json"` and FacebookObjectSearch.java:67 `String searchUrl = "https://graph.facebook.com/search?q=tamil&type=post&access_token="`. So the same codebase demonstrably knows to use https for credentialed API calls and does not on this one path, exposing the api_key to any network observer and allowing the JSON response to be tampered with in transit -- and that response is then parsed and reflected into an HTML page (line 74 `ps.println("")` where farm/server/id/secret come from parser.getString(), e.g. line 82 `secret = parser.getString()`), so an MITM also controls attacker-chosen text inside the emitted HTML. Flagged at LOW confidence for Shape C specifically: unlike lead 1 there is NO hedge comment or other marker that a protection was deliberately disabled or reverted here, so the parallel-path inconsistency is the only signal and this may simply be stale demo code rather than a reverted fix.
evidence: Query (protection-inconsistency sweep -- all three URL literals came back in ONE result set): MATCH (c:CpgCall {scan_id:$scan_id}) WHERE c.code CONTAINS '//' OR c.code CONTAINS '/*' RETURN c.file_path AS file, c.line AS line, left(c.code,300) AS code ORDER BY file, line -> rows include {file: 'demos/rest/src/main/java/org/eclipse/parsson/demos/rest/ParserResource.java', line: 53, code: 'URL url = new URL("http://api.flickr.com/services/rest/?method=flickr.photos.getRecent&api_key=221160312e1c22ec60ecf336951b0e77&format=json&nojsoncallback=1&per_page=20")'}; {file: 'demos/twitter/.../TwitterObjectSearch.java', line: 69, code: 'String searchUrl = "https://api.twitter.com/1.1/search/tweets.json"'}; {file: 'demos/facebook/.../FacebookObjectSearch.java', line: 67, code: 'String searchUrl = "https://graph.facebook.com/search?q=tamil&type=post&access_token="'}. Second query (reachability + the HTML reflection sink fed by the plaintext response): MATCH (c:CpgCall {scan_id:$scan_id}) WHERE toLower(c.code) =~ '(?s).*(trustmanager|...|http://).*' RETURN c.file_path, c.line, c.name, left(c.code,220), c.reachable_from_entry -> ParserResource.java line 53 (.assignment / .alloc / ) reachable_from_entry=true, and line 74 'ps.println("")' reachable_from_entry=true. Third query (confirms the reflected values are parsed from the fetched JSON, and that no escaping is applied): MATCH (c:CpgCall {scan_id:$scan_id}) WHERE toLower(c.code) =~ '(?s).*(escape|encode|sanitiz|html|getwriter|print|append).*' AND c.file_path CONTAINS 'ParserResource' RETURN c.line, c.name, left(c.code,240), c.reachable_from_entry -> line 56 'PrintWriter ps = new PrintWriter(new OutputStreamWriter(os, "UTF-8"))', line 61 'ps.println("")', line 74 the concatenation, line 87 'ps.println("")' -- no escape/encode call present; and from the oauth/secret sweep: line 59 'String secret = null', line 82 'secret = parser.getString()'.

text: BOM magic-byte detection in UnicodeDetectingInputStream.detectEncoding() is gated on `bufLen == 4`, so every BOM literal pattern (NUL/FE/FF/EF/BB/BF) is only ever compared when exactly 4 bytes were buffered. Inputs that buffer 2 or 3 bytes fall straight through to `return StandardCharsets.UTF_8` with curIndex left at 0, meaning the BOM bytes are never consumed and are handed to the JSON tokenizer as content. A 3-byte UTF-8-BOM-only document (EF BB BF) and a 2-byte UTF-16 BOM (FE FF / FF FE) both mis-detect: the UTF-16 cases are silently decoded as UTF-8. The correct gate is `bufLen >= 2` with per-prefix length checks, not an exact-4 equality.
evidence:
Query: MATCH (c:CpgCall {scan_id:$scan_id}) WHERE c.file_path CONTAINS 'UnicodeDetectingInputStream' AND c.line >= 100 AND c.line <= 140 RETURN c.name, c.line, c.code, c.reachable_from_entry ORDER BY c.line
Result: line 105 `bufLen < 2` (throws PARSER_INPUT_ENC_DETECT_FAILED at 106); line 107 `<operator>.equals` with code `bufLen == 4`; line 109 holds the BOM literal comparisons `buf[0] == NUL && buf[1] == NUL && buf[2] == FE && buf[3] == FF` plus fieldAccess to UnicodeDetectingInputStream.NUL / .FE / .FF; line 110 `this.curIndex = 4`. All rows reachable_from_entry=true.

Result: detectEncoding at line 103, reachable_from_entry=true, hop_distance=6, centrality=0.0001617128227566134.

text: Software-composition blind spot: 6 of the 11 declared Dependency nodes carry an unresolved Maven property placeholder as their version string instead of a concrete version — jakarta.annotation-api (${jakarta.annotation-api.version}), jakarta.json (${project.version}), jakarta.json-api (${jakarta.json-api.version}), jakarta.ws.rs-api (${jakarta.ws.rs-api.version}), jakarta.xml.bind-api (${jakarta.xml.bind-api.version}), parsson-media (${project.version}). Any version-matching SCA pass over this manifest cannot evaluate those six components at all, so a known-vulnerable version among them would be silently missed. The verifier should resolve the effective versions from the parent pom's <properties> block / dependencyManagement before concluding the dependency set is clean.
